This study examines the long-term stability of mobile simulations within Mobile Ad-Hoc Networks (MANETs), utilizing the Random Waypoint Mobility Model. We demonstrate that this model ensures asymptotic stochastic stability in simulation frameworks. Building upon this finding, we introduce a novel approach to dynamically adjust packet generation rates, thereby optimizing MANET performance.

This study examines the $K^+K^-$ pair production mechanism in $e^+e^-$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=1.020$ GeV, focusing on the roles of electromagnetic Coulomb interactions and final-state interactions (FSI). The FSI effects are modeled using resonances $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$ within a coupled-channel framework. We compare the theoretical predictions against experimental data from the BESIII collaboration. The Coulomb-only model underestimates the observed $K^+K^-$ invariant mass spectrum; however, the inclusion of FSI significantly improves the agreement. Furthermore, the FSI model accurately reproduces the $K^+K^-$ transverse momentum distribution, whereas the Coulomb-only model fails to do so.

We introduce a straightforward and computationally efficient approach to determine the collective inertia tensor for rotational systems, grounded in the Adiabatic Self-Consistent Constraint (ASCC) method. This approach is validated by applying it to the $^{160}$Hf nucleus, comparing its results with those from the finite-temperature cranking formula. The ASCC method demonstrates Galilean invariance, whereas the cranking formulae do not. Additionally, we compare the dynamic alignment patterns derived from both methods and find that the cranking formulae yield more realistic predictions.

This paper introduces the Abstract Reasoning with Graph Abstractions (ARGA) framework, which addresses program synthesis by converting it into a task of finding a valid path within a graph-based Abstract Program (AP). The framework operates through a two-stage process: first, a graph neural network (GNN) generates a graph representing the abstract program, and subsequently, a sequence-to-sequence model translates this abstract program into a concrete implementation. We evaluated ARGA across two synthesis benchmarks, demonstrating that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to assess the impact of various components within the framework.

This paper examines the long-term dynamics of a nonconservative scalar conservation law featuring a discontinuous flux, where the spatial coefficient undergoes abrupt shifts between two negative values. By applying the maximum principle, we establish the optimal smoothing effect characterized by $H^s \to L^\infty$ with $s = 1/2$. Additionally, we demonstrate the smoothness of solutions for the nonnegative case, where the flux is nonnegative, and derive a logarithmic type smoothing result.

The branching fraction for the decay $B^{0} \rightarrow D_{s}^{-} K^{+}$ has been determined using a sample of $1.06 \times 10^{6}$ $B\bar{B}$ pairs from $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $10.58$ GeV, recorded by the Belle II detector. This determination relies on the known branching fraction of the decay $B^{0} \rightarrow D^{-} \pi^{+}$ and the measured ratio of their yields. The resulting branching fraction is $(2.59 \pm 0.12) \times 10^{-3}$, which aligns with theoretical predictions.

This paper introduces a new uplink/downlink scheduling method for in-band full-duplex (IBFD) networks, which accounts for the spatial distribution of users. By leveraging the spatial dimension, the proposed Multi-User Division scheme with Co-Location-Free (MDD-CF) significantly reduces the number of required pilot signals. The study demonstrates that MDD-CF outperforms both time-division duplexing (TDD) and IBFD schemes that rely on a single pilot sequence in high-mobility environments. Furthermore, the performance of MDD-CF is enhanced by integrating a multi-user division scheme based on user clustering (MDD-CF-UC). Simulation results indicate that MDD-CF-UC surpasses TDD, as well as IBFD and MDD-CF, particularly in high-user density and high-mobility conditions.

This paper introduces a numerical approach to assess privacy guarantees in scenarios where theoretical proofs are absent or insufficiently precise. The method involves simulating the execution of DP algorithms to calculate the resulting privacy loss. By leveraging established numerical techniques, we can now evaluate privacy guarantees in previously challenging settings, such as when data is not independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) or when the mechanism is non-linear. The authors demonstrate this technique by analyzing a differentially private federated learning framework, where the mechanism is non-linear and data points are not i.i.d., a combination for which no existing theoretical bounds are available. The numerical results indicate that the privacy levels in this context are significantly stronger than those predicted by current theoretical analyses.

This paper introduces a new optical technique for space-time block modulation (OTSM) that leverages the Walsh-Hadamard transform (WHT) to enhance efficiency. The proposed OTSM system utilizes a 1-D tree architecture composed of $2^{N-1}$ cascaded Y-junctions and $2^{N-1}$ 50:50 beam splitters, alongside $2^{N-1}$ optical paths. The OTSM process begins by applying WHT to the transmitted symbol vector, followed by propagation through the 1-D tree to the respective output ports. At the receiver, demodulation is achieved by applying the inverse Walsh-Hadamard transform (IWT) to the received symbol vector. The OTSM framework is evaluated using both single and multiple transmit/receiver configurations. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations confirm that this approach offers superior performance compared to conventional OTSM methods that rely on direct WHT-based transmission.

This paper investigates the operator norms of the Fourierier transform and its inverse on the weighted discrete Semigroup algebra $\ell^1(S, \rho)$. Specifically, we demonstrate that when $\rho$ is submultiplicative, the operator norms associated with the Fourierier transform on $\ell^1(S, \rho)$ are equivalent to the maximal operator norms on the associated weighted group $C^*$-algebra $C^*(S, \rho)$. Furthermore, we establish that the maximal operator norms on the Fourierier transform for commutative and abelian groups $C^*(S, \rho)$ are identical to those defined on the corresponding $L^1$ space, $L^1(G, \rho)$.

This study introduces a new methodology for simulating laser melting that integrates a phase-field model with a moving-mesh framework. The approach is validated through simulations of a single melt track on a 316L stainless steel substrate, utilizing thermo-physical parameters derived from a comprehensive literature review. The analysis examines how varying thermo-physical properties influence the oscillatory dynamics of the melt pool. The resulting model successfully replicates the experimentally observed wavy morphology of the melt track.

This paper investigates the potential of Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) to enhance connectivity for smart vehicles (SVs) and other mobile units. We introduce a novel IRS-assisted communication framework where SVs, along with other mobile devices, move freely within an IRS-equipped environment. Specifically, we examine a scenario where SVs opportunistically harvest energy from an IRS-assisted Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) to boost throughput. To maximize the average harvested power, we optimize the phase shifts of the IRS elements, accounting for the mobility of both SVs and the IRS. Our analysis demonstrates that IRS-assisted communication can significantly improve SV performance. Furthermore, we explore the impact of varying IRS deployment positions on harvested power and identify optimal placement strategies. Finally, we validate our findings through numerical simulations.

The study examines the dynamics of the map $f(x) = 1 - \alpha|x-1/2||x-1|$, where the parameter $\alpha$ ranges from $0$ to $2$. This function models the evolution of a population density $x$ over time. The paper analyzes the system's behavior, including its attractors and separatrices, and establishes a correspondence between its symbolic dynamics and those of the map $f(x) = 3x(1-x)$, where $x$ varies between $0$ and $1$.

This study examines the impact of a strong magnetic field on the equation of state (EOS) of spin-polarized strange quark matter, which is crucial for understanding the internal structure of magnetar stars. We employ the MIT bag model to calculate the EOS for this system, subsequently deriving the mass-radius relationship for magnetar objects. Our results indicate that strong magnetic fields significantly soften the EOS of spin-polarized strange quark matter, leading to reduced stellar radii and masses. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of the magnetic field on the maximum mass of the most massive stars, demonstrating that it can suppress the critical mass. Finally, we compare our derived EOS and mass-radius curves with existing empirical data to constrain the value of the bag constant.

Driven by the rapid evolution of deep learning, audio-visual correlation research has seen significant advancement. While recent studies have predominantly focused on learning audio-visual representations, the subsequent utilization of these representations remains underexplored. This paper introduces a novel framework for audio-visual representation learning designed to facilitate downstream tasks. The approach employs a dual-stream architecture to extract features from both modalities, which are then combined into a unified representation. This unified representation is further refined through a contrastive learning module, which aligns the learned features with those of downstream tasks. Additionally, the framework incorporates a contrastive loss function to enhance the discriminative capability of these representations. Extensive experiments across various downstream tasks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces a novel approach to the Linear Ordering Problem (LOP) by leveraging Slater's spectrum. This method significantly reduces the problem's complexity by eliminating redundant nodes and arcs. Furthermore, we present a new class of Slater's inequalities, which extend the known family of valid inequalities for LOP. We also present a specialized branch-and-cut algorithm that integrates these new inequalities to solve the LOP. Empirical results indicate that our algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions on a broad range of instances, particularly those with high non-zero density.

Temporal Property Graphs (TPGs) represent a growing format for storing graph data that includes timestamps, yet existing graph query languages struggle to efficiently handle queries on this format. We introduce temporal regular path queries (tRPs), a new language designed to navigate TGP nodes and edges while respecting temporal constraints. We demonstrate that evaluating these queries is NP-hard, but we also provide a query rewriting method that transforms tRPs into equivalent SQL statements using temporal data structures. This approach leverages the fact that many real-world TGP datasets are temporally consistent, allowing for efficient evaluation. We further present a query optimization strategy that accelerates performance on large-scale data. Empirical results show that our system outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions by a factor of 100x.

Radicals are highly reactive species that play pivotal roles in chemical reactions, making their study essential for advancing our understanding of these fundamental processes. While radical-cation and radical-anion interactions have been extensively investigated, neutral radical collisions remain largely unexplored. This gap is particularly significant regarding the $\text{CH}_3$ radical, which is abundant in interstellar space and vital for astrochemistry, yet its low-temperature scattering behavior has been difficult to study due to the challenges of cooling it to ultracold temperatures. This study reports the first experimental observation of ultracold collisions between $\text{CH}_3$ radicals and hydrogen atoms. By employing a crossed-beam setup that combines a hydrogen maser beam with ultracold $\text{CH}_3$ radicals generated via optical cycling, the researchers achieved a collision temperature of approximately 100 mK. The results reveal that the ultracold scattering cross sections for this system are significantly higher than those predicted by standard quantum mechanical models. These findings offer crucial insights into the mechanisms of radical interactions at ultracold temperatures, potentially guiding the development of new theoretical frameworks.

The Living Swift-XRT Point Source catalogue (LSXC) is a continuously updated, automated system that tracks X-ray sources using Swift's X-ray Telescope (XRT). By leveraging Swift's flexible scheduling, LSXC enables real-time monitoring of sources, a capability essential for observing transient events. The system automatically identifies and catalogs all X-ray sources from Swift's archival data, covering the period from 2005 to the present. LSXC is publicly accessible via an online database, which also provides a web interface for users to search for and request observations of specific targets. This tool is designed to support both the broader astronomical community and professional astronomers.

This study examines how global and country-specific economic shocks influence bilateral trade flows between major trading partners, including the EU, China, India, and the US. Utilizing a dataset spanning 1990 to 2019, we analyze the transmission of these shocks through a Vector Autoregression (VAR) framework. The results indicate that global shocks exert a stronger impact on trade flows than domestic-specific shocks. Furthermore, the response of trade flows to these events is non-monotonic, characterized by a U-shaped trajectory.

This study examines the link between Poisson gauge theories and the semi-classical approximation of noncommutative Yang-Mills theories. We demonstrate that a broad spectrum of Poisson gauge theories emerges as the semi-classical limit of any fully noncommutative gauge theory. Furthermore, we establish that every Poisson gauge theory can be realized as the semi-classical limit of a noncommutative gauge theory, with a specific exception: the 2D Abelian case, which possesses a unique Poisson gauge theory lacking a corresponding noncommutative origin. We also investigate the implications of this relationship for anomalies and discuss how it informs our understanding of the moduli space of Poisson gauge theories.

This study introduces a novel $H_\infty$-based formulation for the optimal static equalization of passive linear quantum systems, offering a streamlined design methodology. By leveraging a generalized maximum-modulus theorem, we establish a lower bound for the $H_\infty$-norm of any equalizer, which is proven to be tight and achievable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this framework aligns with a $H_\infty$-control theory for passive quantum systems, with the $H_\infty$-norm serving as an indicator of the minimum achievable error.

This paper introduces a new approach to monitoring the perception of time passage using wearable sensors, specifically by analyzing continuously recorded physiological signals. The study employs a multi-modal dataset from 15 participants, which includes electrocardiogram (ECG), blood oxygen (SpO2), and accelerometer data. The analysis focuses on two primary tasks: first, identifying specific biomarkers that reflect time passage, and second, developing a model to continuously monitor changes in time perception using these markers. The proposed method utilizes a multi-modal Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract time perception-related features from the raw signals. The results demonstrate that the CNN successfully identifies distinct biomarkers, including heart rate variability (HRV), SpO2, and acceleration metrics, which are effective for tracking time passage. Furthermore, a novel CNN architecture is presented that enables the continuous monitoring of time perception by leveraging these identified biomarkers.

The drift-diffusion model (DDM) is a foundational framework for modeling decision-making under uncertainty, positing that decisions emerge from the gradual integration of evidence toward a threshold. Although the DDM has been extensively utilized in psychology and neuroscience, it has seen little application in artificial intelligence. This study introduces a neural network architecture that implements the DDM, demonstrating its ability to replicate human performance on the visual search task. By comparing the network's behavior with human data, the research reveals that the network's performance is constrained by the same limitations found in human observers.

The legal field has recently begun adopting machine learning (ML) fairness concepts, creating a need for dialogue between communities to align their respective definitions and terminology. This paper examines conflicts between legal language and fairness vocabularies, arguing that the ML side stands to gain more from resolving these terminological discrepancies than the legal community. We introduce a framework for mapping and analyzing the semantic relationships between fairness definitions, demonstrating that current machine learning definitions frequently fail to align with legal fairness concepts. To address this misalignment, we propose a novel definition of fairness that achieves a meaningful synergy between academic and legal terminologies.

This study introduces a novel detection technique for neutrinos based on the inverse process of radiative neutrino pair emission. We demonstrate that this mechanism generates a detectable magnetization within the target material. By utilizing a high-intensity photon beam passing through a target within a strong magnetic field, our proposed method offers a direct and highly sensitive means of detecting neutrinos produced via the light-by-lights scattering process. This approach is applicable to searches for both standard model and beyond-standard-model (BSM) three-neutrino mixing, as well as for detecting $\nu\bar{\nu}$ pairs generated by virtual heavy particles such as $Z'$ bosons or dark matter candidates. Furthermore, our analysis establishes that the proposed method is capable of probing the neutrino interaction cross-section down to the $10^{-38} \text{ cm}^2$ level.

This study examines the charge symmetry breaking (CSB) splitting within the multiplets of hypernuclei $^{7}\Lambda$H and $^{8}\Lambda$H, where H represents a hydrogen-like nucleus. The analysis employs a microscopic framework utilizing the $\Lambda N$ interaction, which incorporates both isospin non-conserving terms and the Coulomb force. The resulting CSB splittings are found to be substantial, with values of approximately 100 keV for $^{7}\Lambda$H and 200 keV for $^{8}\Lambda$H. Furthermore, the calculated CSB splitting in $^{7}\Lambda$H aligns well with the experimental data.

Social media platforms utilize algorithms to deliver personalized content, but users can manipulate these systems by strategically posting to skew their inferred profiles. This paper investigates such misrepresentation in the context of Twitter's recommendation engine. We introduce a straightforward yet effective strategy for deceiving the system, demonstrating that it is feasible to alter the system's perception of a user's interests and habits without altering their actual activity or bio. We validate this approach through experiments on the Twitter API, utilizing a dataset of 10,000 accounts. Results indicate that 98% of the test subjects could be successfully profile-misled, with 95% of those requiring fewer than 100 manipulated tweets to achieve the desired effect.

The Kingman coalescent, a cornerstone of population genetics, is traditionally defined by the independence of the random times associated with each coalescent event. This study re-examines the process by examining how offspring distributions influence event independence. We demonstrate that the independence of these times is contingent upon the specific functional form of the offspring distribution, noting that independence does not universally hold for all such functions. For instance, when offspring distributions are binomial, the resulting independence is only approximate, whereas it is strictly independent under a uniform distribution. Additionally, we observe that the process can be characterized by a continuous-time Markov chain with a state space representing partitions of integers. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of this Markov chain as time extends infinitely.

This study constructs Gibbs measures for a hard-core model on the Cayley tree featuring a countable set of parameters, derived from an irreducible non-negative matrix with an associated spectral radius.

We introduce a novel method for determining the central velocity dispersion ($\sigma_0$) of early-type galaxies (ETGs) using LAMOST's low-resolution spectra. This approach involves fitting the observed spectra with synthetic templates generated by the E-MILES library, which accounts for the effects of spatial resolution. We applied this technique to 1,000 ETGs previously analyzed by the SDSS-BOSS survey, comparing our results with those derived from the Fitting Kinematics and Dynamics of Galaxies (FKD) pipeline. The comparison reveals that our LAMOST-derived $\sigma_0$ values align well with FKD results, with a median discrepancy of only 1.4% and a standard deviation of 10.6%. Furthermore, our method enables the calculation of $\sigma_0$ for 1,000 ETGs observed by the DESI Legacy Survey (LS), which were inaccessible to the SDSS-BOSS survey. When comparing these new measurements with those from the SDSS-BOSS sample, we find that the median difference is 1.4% with a standard deviation of 10.6%. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the central velocity dispersion and the galaxy's mass-to-light ratio, finding that the median difference between the two samples is 1.4% with a standard deviation of 10.6%. This study introduces a streamlined methodology for computing isotope shifts within relativistic coupled-cluster theory, utilizing analytical energy derivatives. By leveraging the established framework of analytic derivative techniques to evaluate nuclear size effects, the approach eliminates the need for additional third-order derivatives of the energy. We demonstrate that this method yields results identical to those obtained via conventional derivative techniques, while offering significant efficiency gains in both memory usage and computational speed. Furthermore, the method's accuracy is validated through comparisons with high-precision calculations performed using standard procedures.

This study examines how local symplectic groups act on binary symmetric matrices. We demonstrate that the orbits of the local symplectic group are indistinguishable from those of the local general linear group. This equivalence yields an explicit matrix representation for elements of the local symplectic group and establishes that both groups possess isomorphic normalizers of their respective standard filtrations.

Let $G$ be a graph partitioned into two sets, $A$ and $B$. This paper establishes that for any bipartite graph $G$ devoid of 4-cycles, a matching of cardinality $|A|$ is guaranteed to exist provided every vertex in $A$ possesses a degree strictly exceeding $2/3$ of $|B|$. This finding resolves an inquiry originally posed by Alon, F\"uredi, and Tuza.

Cloud services are increasingly utilized to deliver video streaming services, with the primary goal of maintaining Quality of Service (QoS) by dynamically adjusting video quality in response to fluctuating network conditions. This paper introduces a new framework for dynamic video streaming that leverages cloud capabilities to ensure QoS. The proposed framework employs a two-stage approach: initially, it utilizes a predictive model to estimate the available bandwidth for each user, followed by the selection of an appropriate video bitrate based on that prediction. Subsequently, it adapts the video bitrate in real-time to align with actual network bandwidth. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework effectively maintains QoS by dynamically adjusting video quality.

This study examines the extreme behavior of random variables representing cycle densities in Erd\H{o}s-R\H{e}nyi graphs, defined by $n$ vertices and edge probability $p$. We introduce a dichotomy based on deviation magnitude relative to $n$: small deviations, scaled by $O(n)$, adhere to a Poisson distribution, whereas large deviations, scaled by $n^\alpha$ where $\alpha > 1$, follow a Gaussian normal distribution. The paper further analyzes the transition between these regimes and establishes a universal law for deviating cycle densities when the deviation scales as $n p^{k-1} (\log(1/p))^{\alpha}$, where $k$ corresponds to the average shortest cycle length and $\alpha$ is a constant specific to $k$.

This paper establishes the Morse index stability for the ground state with a cubic nonlinearity in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for dimensions $d \in \{1, 2\}$. The work also derives Morse index lower bounds applicable to higher-dimensional cases.

Proof-based simulation offers a method to formally verify the properties of stochastic systems, enabling the establishment of rigorous bounds on their behavior. This paper introduces a novel framework for applying proof-by-techniques to statistical design, a strategy that yields verifiable constraints regarding the design's operating parameters. The core of this approach involves a new algorithm for generating and verifying inductive invariants within continuous-time Markov chains. This algorithm operates by synthesizing candidate invariants through a series of simulations, subsequently validating them via proof-by-stimulation. The resulting theory is implemented in a dedicated tool, which we employ to verify a previously unproven hypothesis concerning the characteristics of a specific statistical design.

Cloud computing has become a vital component of modern digital infrastructure, enabling the delivery of complex applications over the internet. Remote rendering, which offloads graphics processing to centralized servers, is a key application of this paradigm, promising to make high-end graphics accessible to users with modest hardware. However, network latency remains a critical obstacle to the user experience in cloud-based remote rendering. To address this, we introduce a new approach that leverages network coding to deliver multiple video streams concurrently, thereby reducing the impact of latency. We evaluated this method using a testbed featuring a latency of 100ms and a packet loss rate of 1%. Results indicate that our network-coded solution outperforms traditional methods, delivering a 1.5x speedup in rendering latency and a 1.5x reduction in end-to-end delay.

This study introduces a novel audio-to-audio alignment method that leverages the interplay between visual and audio modalities. The proposed approach utilizes a differentiable, audio-driven deformable grid to synchronize audio features from a reference track with those of a performance. By integrating a visual score derived from the performance, this grid is optimized to create a precise audio-to-audio alignment. The framework is designed to be model-agnostic, allowing it to function with various audio feature representations. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that this method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of alignment accuracy.

Full-duplex transceivers are essential for realizing the potential of future wireless networks, yet their implementation remains challenging due to the necessity of suppressing both linear and nonlinear self-interference. This paper introduces a novel self-interference mitigation technique that leverages the inherent properties of self-interference to achieve cancellation. The proposed method utilizes a dual approach: first, it employs a tunable delay to create a time-domain echo, and subsequently, it applies a time-varying filter to introduce time-dependent attenuation. By dynamically adjusting these two parameters, the system can effectively mitigate both linear and nonlinear self-interference. The study further details the design of a low-complexity, hardware-friendly implementation and presents experimental results demonstrating the method's efficacy.

We propose a framework to describe the final morphology of dried colloidal droplets by applying mechanical principles to the resulting solid. This approach models the solid as a thin, heterogeneous shell situated within a viscoelastic substrate, where the shell's internal stress arises from differential shrinkage. By utilizing the framework of shell mechanics, we derive a simple criterion for shell buckling based on the strain gradient across the shell's thickness. This model accurately predicts the observed buckling patterns in various colloidal systems, including different types of coffee rings, polymer latex suspensions, and inkjet-printed droplets.

This study examines the evolution of dust disks in the star-forming region NGC 2071, utilizing high-resolution ALMA data at 3.1 mm and 1.3 mm. The results reveal a complex, multi-ring structure, with the innermost ring (Ring 1) showing a distinct correlation between the UV-CO band intensity and the Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) radiation field. This relationship supports the hypothesis that the UV-CO band serves as a reliable tracer for the Ly$\alpha$ radiation environment. Furthermore, the innermost ring exhibits a strong correlation with the star-forming regions, suggesting that the ring's morphology is driven by the combined effects of stellar feedback and the gravitational potential of the star-forming complex. In contrast, the outer rings (Ring 2 and Ring 3) lack a significant correlation with either the star-forming regions or the Ly$\alpha$ radiation field. Consequently, the formation of these outer rings is likely attributed to other mechanisms, such as the influence of the spiral arms of the star-forming region.

This study introduces a novel algorithm, termed Residual Convolution Network Regression (RCNR), designed to address the challenge of estimating three-dimensional positions for multiple users. The approach begins by employing a deep neural network to learn a residual mapping from the initial coarse position estimates to the final fine-grained corrections. Subsequently, a deep regression network is utilized to predict the residual position errors, thereby refining the overall localization accuracy. The RCNR method is validated through extensive simulations, demonstrating significant performance gains over existing techniques.

This study examines the quantum interference of rotating particles within a magnetic solenoid, focusing on the geometric phase. We demonstrate that the phase remains well-defined near the central axis of the solenoid, whereas uncertainty increases with distance from the center. We further elucidate the physical origins of phase uncertainty and discuss its potential observational consequences.

This study examines the pricing strategies of electric vehicle (EV) charging stations, balancing profitability with customer satisfaction. We introduce a model where a charging station sets prices for energy and power, while EVs adjust their arrival times and departure schedules to minimize individual costs. The analysis focuses on scenarios where customers are aware of prices but cannot influence them, contrasting this with a scenario where prices are fixed by the customer. We demonstrate that the resulting EV behaviors and pricing decisions form a Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish that the charging station's profit function is concave in the first scenario and the customer's cost function is convex in the second, ensuring the existence of a unique optimal solution for the charging station's price in the first scenario. Finally, we compare the outcomes of both scenarios to evaluate the impact of customer flexibility on the charging station's earnings.

This paper investigates the optimal design function, which determines treatment probabilities to minimize the variance of a randomized experiment's average treatment effect (ATE) estimator. We demonstrate that this optimal design varies based on the distribution of the running variable, the variable used to assign treatment. Specifically, under certain conditions, the estimator can be minimized using either a "bang-bang" design function, which assigns treatment probabilistically only at the boundaries, or a linear design function, which assigns treatment probabilistically linearly across the range. We provide sufficient conditions for the optimality of each design and offer a practical algorithm to identify which design type applies. Additionally, we present a regression discontinuity design (RDD) framework that accommodates multiple treatments, where treatment assignment is determined by proximity to a cutoff. We show that, under specific constraints, these multi-treatment RDDs can also be optimized to minimize ATE estimator variance, with the resulting optimal designs being either linear or "bang-bang" depending on whether the design is above or below the threshold. Finally, we illustrate these concepts with a case study on a randomized experiment from the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) that evaluated the impact of a job training program.

This work investigates the two-point correlation functions of two conserved current multiplets within the context of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories. By applying the superconformal Ward identities, we determine the corresponding structure constants for the associated four-point functions of the multiplets' primary operators. The resulting correlation functions for the conserved current multiplets are determined up to an overall normalization factor, which depends on the ranks of the multiplets. We also examine the constraints imposed by unitarity on these correlation functions.

Machine teaching is a learning-focused variation of machine learning that enables learners to instruct algorithms on how to acquire information. Although existing machine teaching tools typically focus on adult users, this research explores how to create interfaces tailored for children. We conducted a study involving 21 children aged 8 to 12 to identify key interface elements that support their understanding of machine learning concepts, such as data, training, and generalization. Additionally, we examined how children perceive the relationship between teaching strategies and the resulting learned concepts. Our findings indicate that children value the ability to visualize and manipulate data, as well as the capacity to experiment with teaching strategies. Furthermore, we observed that children often struggle to distinguish between generalization and memorization, frequently confusing the two. Based on these insights, we propose a machine teaching interface that incorporates these features and evaluate its effectiveness through a pilot study with 16 children.

Lifelong learning is a rapidly evolving field that aims to enable systems to continuously acquire new knowledge while retaining previously acquired information. This study introduces a lifelong learning framework specifically designed for trial-and-error interactions, where the system must select actions to maximize cumulative rewards. We propose a lifelong reinforcement learning approach that utilizes a specific loss function to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Our method is evaluated on the Rocksample environment, demonstrating that it outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines.

Quantum coherence is a vital resource for quantum information processing, yet it is often lost when quantum states change their degree of freedom (DoF), such as during the transformation from polarization to time-bin or path encoding. This study demonstrates that quantum coherence can be preserved across DoFs by utilizing a DoF-independent decoherence mechanism. We show that this preservation occurs because the decoherence generated by a random phase shift on a single photon remains invariant regardless of which specific DoF is being used. This finding offers a new perspective on quantum coherence, suggesting that its stability across DoFs can be leveraged to develop more effective strategies for quantum information transfer.

This study examines the single-molecule unbinding of a DNA hairpin induced by a biasing force, with the DNA modeled as a Markov chain. We derive the unbinding time distribution and the corresponding single-molecule current, establishing a closed-form solution for the current. Our analysis demonstrates that the current remains an exponential function of the applied bias, a property that arises from the two-state nature of the system. Furthermore, we prove that the unbinding time distribution is characterized by a single exponential, with its mean inversely proportional to the bias. Our analytical results are validated through numerical simulations.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework for real-time multi-view registration, prioritizing computational efficiency and robustness over peak accuracy. The proposed method leverages a deep learning architecture to perform pairwise view matching and utilizes the resulting correspondences to estimate relative poses via the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm. Specifically, we employ a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to generate feature maps for each view, which are subsequently processed by a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to establish point matches. The resulting robust performance in pose estimation is validated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study examines the geometric characteristics of mappings linked to optimization problems within Hilbert spaces, specifically demonstrating that the mapping introduced by Attouch and Swoboda in 2000 is bi-Lipschitzian. Furthermore, we establish conditions for its bi-regularity and prove its regularized version to be both bi-Lipschitzian and strongly regular. These findings are applied to address the existence of solutions for Attouch and Swoboda's mathematical program.

This study examines the matrix model defined by the potential $V(z)=z^p+\alpha z^2+\beta z$, where $p$ is an odd integer, focusing on the regime where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are small. We demonstrate that the scaling behavior of the free energy's vanishing order in this limit is governed by a quadratic equation, one of whose roots corresponds to the exponent in the large-$N$ scaling law for the free energy. This finding is linked to the breaking of conformal symmetry, which emerges in the model when $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are non-zero. Specifically, we show that the scaling exponent for the two-point function of the holomorphic primary field is identical to the root of the quadratic equation that dictates the free energy's scaling. Furthermore, we prove that the conformal dimension of the specific primary field associated with the deformation term $z^p$ matches the exponent describing the free energy's scaling.

This study examines the dynamical evolution of a four-dimensional system comprising two colliding, identical phase domains characterized by opposite chirality. The analysis focuses on how varying collision velocity and domain size influence the resulting dynamics. The research demonstrates that both parameters significantly affect the outcome, leading to distinct regimes: at low velocities and large sizes, domains grow and merge into a homogeneous state; conversely, at high velocities and small sizes, they annihilate one another. Furthermore, the findings indicate that dynamical behavior is not solely dictated by size and velocity but is also contingent on the specific initial phase configuration.

This paper introduces BCF, a novel framework for safe robotics exploration and deployment that leverages Bayesian inference to model the robot's belief over the environment. Built upon a probabilistic transition model, BCF utilizes Bayesian inference to generate a posterior distribution of possible states, thereby capturing uncertainty. By sampling from this posterior, BCF enables the robot to safely interact with its surroundings. To maximize interaction value, the framework employs an information-theoretic metric to assess the informativeness of each state. Additionally, to ensure deployment safety, BCF utilizes a probabilistic safety barrier to filter out states that could lead to unsafe conditions. The approach is validated through simulations involving a robotic manipulator performing tasks in a 2D workspace and a mobile robot navigating a 3D environment.

This study introduces a new deep learning framework designed to select the arterial input function (AIF) from cerebral perfusion imaging data. The proposed method utilizes a neural network to identify the optimal region of interest (ROI) for the AIF by analyzing the initial 15 seconds of dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) or perfusion CT (CT perfusion) data. This approach is particularly advantageous for DCE-MRI, where the AIF is typically derived from the first few minutes of the scan. By leveraging the initial data, the method allows for the analysis of the remainder of the scan to generate more precise estimates of tissue perfusion parameters. The model was trained on a dataset comprising 100 DCE-MRI scans and 100 CT perfusion scans, with the performance of the trained network evaluated on an independent test set. The results demonstrate that the method achieves high accuracy in ROIs selection, with a mean absolute error of 1.9% for DCE-MRI and 1.2% for CT perfusion.

Partial fraction identities are essential for computing quantities in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), such as splitting functions, anomalous dimensions, and soft functions. This paper introduces a new algorithm designed to extract these relationships from general color structures. The method leverates the gauge invariant nature of physical observables and applies a generalized version of the color algebra technique. We demonstrate the method's capabilities through examples involving up to four particles, utilizing the color algebra of $\mathfrak{su}(N_c)$.

This paper investigates the chordal properties of power graphs within finite groups. By characterizing the finite groups that possess chordal power graphs—specifically identifying them as cyclic, prime-order, or prime-squared order—we also establish that the lattice of subgroups for these specific groups is chordal.

This paper introduces a new method for single-channel target source separation, termed Optimal Condition Training (OCT). By leveraging the principle that a neural network's performance is enhanced when its input conditions are more favorable, OCT optimizes the training data to boost separation efficacy. The approach utilizes a mask estimator to generate superior input masks for a subsequent spectral estimator, a process repeated iteratively. Experiments on the WSJ0-2mix dataset demonstrate that OCT achieves a 1.1 dB improvement in Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR) compared to standard training. The methodology is also applicable to multi-channel scenarios, where it yields a 1.0 dB SI-SDR gain on the MUSAN dataset.

This paper examines the metrological capabilities of quantum states within the class of block incoherent states, demonstrating that their quantum Fisher information can be expressed using a sum of independent contributions from each block. We introduce a set of optimal measurement strategies for estimating parameters that vary linearly across the states in this class. Additionally, we analyze the performance of these states under the linear noise model, deriving upper and lower bounds for the mean square error in parameter estimation. These results are further illustrated through specific examples.

We present a new analysis of the H 1743-322 hard state using the recently introduced QPO fractional rms model, which incorporates the QPO's frequency dependence. This approach reveals that the QPO fractional rms during the decay phase is significantly lower than in the rise phase at low frequencies, a discrepancy that diminishes as frequency increases. These findings align with the hypothesis that the QPO originates in the corona, with the observed shift in the decay phase rms indicating a change in the corona's location. Furthermore, the data suggest that the corona's position is contingent upon the accretion flow's structure.

This study introduces an extractive question answering system designed for Romanian, a low-resource language. The approach relies on a bi-encoder architecture that leverages pre-trained contextualized word embeddings from BERT. To address the scarcity of Romanian BERT data, we developed a new pre-trained model named RoBERTe, which was trained on a corpus of 10 billion words. The experimental results demonstrate that our RoBERTe-based extractive system outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods on the Romanian Open-domain Question Answering dataset.

The distribution of baryons in the local universe is hypothesized to mirror the Cosmic Web's structure. This study investigates the filamentary architecture of the local universe by analyzing the distribution of galaxies and the intergalactic medium (IGM) across a 1000 Mpc/h³ volume. We employ the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) Data Release 12 (DR12) galaxy catalog, utilizing the 3D Delaunay tessellation method to map the IGM's density field based on Lyman-alpha forest data from the BOSS eBOSS sample. We present a novel technique for identifying filaments in the IGM that accounts for the observational line-of-sight (LOS) effect. By applying this method to the combined galaxy and IGM datasets, we successfully reconstructed the local Cosmic Web. We further examined the influence of varying galaxy samples on the resulting filamentary structures, demonstrating that the local Cosmic Web's morphology remains robust against variations in galaxy sample selection.

Treewidth is a fundamental parameter in graph theory, and a key challenge is to approximate it within a polynomial time frame. While previous algorithms required a runtime of $2^{O(k)} \cdot n^{O(1)}$—dependent on the input size $k$—this work introduces a superior method with a runtime of $2^{O(\alpha)} \cdot n^{O(1)}$, where $\alpha$ denotes the treewidth of the graph. This approach utilizes a combination of treewidth decomposition and the technique of graph sparsification.

Tidal Disruption Events (TDEs) are infrequent galactic phenomena where a star is torn apart by a massive black hole. While the majority of TDEs are observed in the outskirts of galaxies, the central regions of post-starburst galaxies (PSGs) offer a unique setting to investigate the potential for TDEs. This is because PSGs typically contain a population of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) and a high density of main sequence stars, making them ideal candidates for such events. This study introduces a new deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for optimizing resource block allocation in cellular networks. By integrating actor-critic learning, our approach offers significant advantages over conventional scheduling methods, such as Maximum Rate and Proportional Fairness. Specifically, the system demonstrates superior performance in terms of both fairness and efficiency, while also exhibiting greater robustness against fluctuations in channel conditions and user mobility. Furthermore, the proposed DRL scheduler is capable of adapting to diverse network environments, including those with varying traffic loads and differing user priorities.

This paper introduces refined word-level quality estimation (QE) by addressing the inherent ambiguity of assigning a single QE score to each word. Unlike standard QE approaches, our method allows for multiple scores to characterize a word, offering greater flexibility. We introduce a straightforward yet effective framework that integrates various QE scores into a single word representation. Furthermore, we propose a new evaluation metric to assess the performance of this refined approach. Experimental results demonstrate that the refined method outperforms the original QE in both machine translation and natural language generation.

This study investigates the geometric properties of a recently proposed Kerr--de Sitter black hole, which differs from the traditional model by incorporating an additional parameter. This new dimensionless parameter, which is zero in the standard model, is derived from the charge of a scalar field. We analyze how this parameter influences the black hole's shadow geometry, noting that it alters the shadow's shape and position while leaving its size unchanged. Furthermore, we examine the impact of this parameter on photon trajectories, specifically their precession and deflection.

This study introduces a novel flux-conservative formulation of general relativistic hydrodynamics, designed to enhance the precision of numerical simulations. The approach decomposes the evolution equations into a set of hyperbolic partial differential equations, where the primary innovation involves the inclusion of a source term within the fluxes. This modification ensures that numerical fluxes remain well-defined at cell interfaces, thereby eliminating the need for extrapolating source terms. The accuracy gains are achieved by aligning the relativistic hydrodynamic equations with the standard form of hyperbolic systems, resulting in faster numerical convergence. The efficacy of this new framework is validated through simulations of a collapsing scalar field, a relativistic shock tube, and a binary neutron star merger.

This paper outlines a method to estimate the fractal dimensions for functions defined on the Sierpiński Gasket (SG). This method is applicable to a broad spectrum of functions, encompassing those that are discontinuous, as well as those that are not Hölder continuous. The text also presents a novel definition for the graph dimension, along with corresponding theorems that allow for the calculation of this dimension for specific function classes.

This study investigates the impact of guiding image-based question generation models on their output quality. While recent advances in this field have achieved high-quality results, they often suffer from grammatical incoherence and lack of relevance. To address this, we introduce a method that constrains the question generation process by selecting a relevant image region and directing the model accordingly. Our approach utilizes a pre-trained vision-language model to identify the image region of interest, which is then converted into a visual feature vector. This vector serves as input to the model, steering the resulting question toward the targeted area. Experimental results demonstrate that this guidance mechanism notably enhances both grammatical correctness and image relevance.

We analyze a sample of 1,000 isolated halos, each ranging from $10^{9}$ to $10^{10} M_\odot$ in mass and located at $z=0$. The core radius is defined as the distance from the halo center where the density drops to half its central value. We observe a strong correlation between the dark matter core size and the host halo's stellar mass, a relationship that remains robust across various stellar mass-to-light ratios and initial conditions. Furthermore, we observe that the core sizes of these halos are nearly identical to those of the most massive subhalos within the larger $10^{12} M_\odot$ host halo in the simulation, suggesting that halo cores are established during the initial assembly of the most massive subhalos. Quasipure variables represent a refined extension of the traditional pure variable concept, and this study introduces an efficient algorithm to eliminate them within DPLL frameworks. We demonstrate that quasipure elimination proves more effective than its pure counterpart, with the method being compatible for integration into any existing SAT solver. This paper further introduces a novel heuristic for determining the optimal variable to eliminate and evaluates the approach through rigorous experimental analysis.

The Folk Theorem for evolutionary games posits that any feasible and individually rational payoff vector can be sustained as a Nash equilibrium within non-zero-sum games. This theoretical framework has been instrumental in elucidating the dynamics of natural selection and predicting behaviors across diverse biological and social systems. However, the theorem's reliance on unbounded, open-ended strategies renders it inapplicable to many real-world scenarios, particularly those constrained by limited memory. This paper addresses that limitation by demonstrating that a broad spectrum of both bounded and open-ended outcomes can indeed be maintained as equilibria in games featuring short-memory strategies. Our findings offer a robust method for modeling evolutionary game theory in contexts where strategies are inherently limited.

This paper introduces a Multivariate Regression Tree (MRT) designed to model the conditional distribution of a multivariate response vector given a univariate predictor. MRT constructs a hierarchical tree structure, where each terminal node's estimated distributions are mutually independent. By employing a multivariate mixture model, the method captures the full conditional distribution, enabling the calculation of probabilities for multivariate events. The authors present a new algorithm for determining optimal partitioning variables and thresholds within the regression tree. This algorithm utilizes a two-stage approach: first identifying candidate split locations, then selecting the best split among them. The study also introduces a new variable selection criterion that integrates the correlation structure of the multivariate response into tree growth. Simulations demonstrate that this methodology outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy.

This paper introduces a new charging algorithm for a fleet of electric vehicles (EVs) that integrates both predictive control and reinforcement learning. The proposed method is Communication-Censored (CC), designed to minimize communications between the fleet and the central server. By leveraging a predictive controller as a baseline, the CC strategy ensures that the system remains stable and near-optimal even if communication occurs only rarely. The primary objective is to minimize the aggregate waiting time for all EVs, while adhering to constraints regarding total charging power and the state of charge for individual vehicles. To achieve this, the paper proposes a CC policy that utilizes a communication-based, model-free algorithm to learn and optimize the parameters of the predictive controller. The system is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to facilitate the theoretical analysis of the CC policy's performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the CC policy outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios with limited communication bandwidth.

This study examines how the density functional choice influences the electronic properties of the $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ material. We compare the performance of various functionals, including PBE, PBE0, HSE06, and HCT, by analyzing their effects on the band structure, density of states, and optical conductivity. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of spin-orbit coupling on the band structure and electronic states. The findings indicate that while band structure characteristics are relatively consistent across these methods, the density of states and optical conductivity exhibit notable variations.

The gut microbiome's functional capabilities are a key determinant of its resilience to environmental changes. However, the extent to which specific functional traits vary across different ecological niches within the microbiome remains unclear. This study employed a multi-omics approach to examine the metabolic landscape of the gut microbiome in a cohort of 100 individuals, revealing that the metabolic niche space is highly structured and stratified by distinct habitats and host species. Notably, the niche space is shaped by a combination of intrinsic factors, including host genetics, and extrinsic factors, including diet. Furthermore, the niche space is organized along a distinct axis that correlates with the degree of microbial community specialization. Collectively, these results indicate that the functional composition of the microbiome is organized into a complex, multi-layered structure that is both intrinsically and extrinsically regulated.

This paper introduces a new approach for analyzing and monitoring building systems by employing symbolic representations of sensor data. The proposed method utilizes the Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAX) algorithm to convert continuous data streams into symbolic patterns, which are subsequently used to construct specific models. The study evaluates the proposed method's performance using real-world data from a building's HVAC system, demonstrating its effectiveness in fault detection and diagnosis.

Binary interactions are crucial for the evolution of massive stars, particularly in generating hydrogen-poor Type II supernovae (SNe II). This study examines the impact of mass transfer on the evolution of massive binary systems, utilizing the MESA stellar evolution code. We modeled the formation of hydrogen-poor SNe II by simulating mass transfer scenarios where the donor star is a rapidly rotating massive star. Our results indicate that mass transfer can significantly alter the evolution of both donor and accretor stars. Specifically, the accretor's mass increases, while the donor star's evolution accelerates, leading to earlier core collapse. We analyzed how varying mass transfer rates influence the donor's mass loss and the resulting donor and accretor properties. Our findings suggest that mass transfer rates of approximately $10^{-3} M_{\odot} \text{yr}^{-1}$ are sufficient to strip the hydrogen envelope from the donor, creating conditions favorable for hydrogen-poor SNe II. Additionally, we observed that the accretor's mass growth rate correlates with the mass transfer rate, and the donor's mass loss rate is contingent on the accretion efficiency.

This study examines how temperature affects magnetization switching in 2D magnets, utilizing a modified Stoner-Wohlfarth model that incorporates both an external field and thermal fluctuations. The analysis focuses on the time-dependent switching probability as a function of magnetization orientation relative to the easy axis and the applied field strength. By comparing switching times at finite temperatures with those at zero temperature, the work elucidates the mechanisms of thermally assisted switching. The results indicate that thermal activation significantly accelerates switching when the magnetization is perpendicular to the field, whereas it merely prolongs the switching time for initial conditions aligned with the easy axis.

We introduce a fresh, visually grounded approach to syntax modeling that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Our model utilizes a recurrent neural network to predict the next syntactic category based on visual context, while simultaneously predicting the most probable tree structure for an image. This framework achieves superior results compared to previous constituency induction techniques, including those employing contrastive learning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these visually grounded models can effectively leverage synthetic data to significantly boost performance.

This study examines the stability of attribution metrics across different datasets. We evaluate five metrics—Integrated Gradients, Gradient×Input, Gradient×Gradient, LIME, and SHAP—across 100 image classification tasks using the ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and MNIST datasets. Our findings indicate that metrics performing well on one dataset often perform poorly on others, suggesting that current attribution metrics are not stable across varying data distributions. To address this, we introduce a new metric, SHAP-CIFAR, designed specifically for the CIFAR-10 dataset. We demonstrate that this metric exhibits greater stability than the other five methods when applied to the same dataset.
